chain.g: dull, foolish, erring, heretical; foolish, silly; presumptuous

ety.text: From Middle English dull, dul (also dyll, dill, dwal), from Old English dol (“dull, foolish, erring, heretical; foolish, silly; presumptuous”), from Proto-West Germanic *dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz, from earlier *dwulaz, a variant of *dwalaz (“stunned, mad, foolish, misled”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwel-, *dʰewel- (“to dim, dull, cloud, make obscure, swirl, whirl”).
Probably from Irish dul, dol (“loop, noose, snare”).

senses.d: Lacking the ability to cut easily; not sharp.
ex: All these knives are dull.
He sat through the dull lecture and barely stayed awake.

senses.d: Not shiny; having a matte finish or no particular luster or brightness.
ex: Choose a dull finish to hide fingerprints.
a dull fire or lamp;  a dull red or yellow;  a dull mirror

senses.d: Not bright or intelligent; stupid; having slow understanding.
ex: She is not bred so dull but she can learn.
dull at classical learning
This people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing.
O, help my weak wit and sharpen my dull tongue.
I felt dull all day.
It's a dull day.
Think me not / So dull a devil to forget the loss / Of such a matchless wife.

c. 1857', Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Table-Talk
As turning the logs will make a dull fire burn, so changes of study a dull brain.
the dull earth

senses.d: Not intense; felt indistinctly or only slightly.
ex: Pressing on the bruise produces a dull pain.

senses.d: To render dull; to remove or blunt an edge or something that was sharp.
ex: Years of misuse have dulled the tools.
This […] dulled their swords.

senses.d: To soften, moderate or blunt; to make dull, stupid, or sluggish; to stupefy.
ex: He drinks to dull the pain.
Those [drugs] she has / Will stupefy and dull the sense a while.

senses.d: To lose a sharp edge; to become dull.
ex: A razor will dull with use.

senses.d: To render dim or obscure; to sully; to tarnish.
A noose of string, metal wire, or hair used to snare an animal, especially a fish.
ex: Play fair, boys. No dynamite nor "dulling." The deadly "dull," or wire noose, is a fatal weapon against a trout.

senses.d: To fish (or snare an animal, especially a fish) with such a noose.
ex: I hope that the barbarous practice called dulling has gone out of fashion.
Play fair, boys. No dynamite nor "dulling." The deadly "dull," or wire noose, is a fatal weapon against a trout.
